proposals.relationship: Higham uses Hofstadter’s The Age of Reform as a specific example of how postwar historians revised the relationship between reform movements and historical change.
proposals.evidence_note: The1959 paragraph beginning For one thing identifies Hofstadter’s influential1955 book, contrasts its treatment of Populism/Progressivism with its account of the New Deal, and uses this as evidence for changed periodization. This is a bounded historiographical resource, not proof Higham adopted every interpretation or equated Hofstadter with Boorstin’s approving conservatism. His paragraph notes the paradox of recognizing radical recent change; the principal extended criticism targets Boorstin. Hofstadter’s book itself unread.
primary_locators: 1959 publisher essay, paragraph beginning For one thing, current scholarship, naming The Age of Reform (1955), and final three paragraphs beginning The advantages / Moreover / It is not likely.

proposals.relationship: Higham argues that the Progressive framework associated jointly with Turner, Beard and Parrington absorbed social-conflict themes while its national assumptions constrained American historians’ engagement with Marxism.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1989 argument462–463 names all three and assigns Beard the leading role in adapting social conflict; Turner is one member of the criticized collective, not sole originator. Higham distinguishes Progressive nationalism from Marxist internationalism and argues their appeal helped marginalize Marxism. His1959 appreciation of earlier moral engagement and institutional revision remains; this later specific criticism is not inferred from the broad existing field edge1472. Turner’s own work unread.
primary_locators: 1989 printed462, paragraphs beginning In addition to the patterns / Paradoxically / The sharpest difference; continuation463 opening and note5.

proposals.relationship: Higham explicitly adapts the language of paradigm while defining it more loosely than Kuhn’s usage for his account of changing American historiography.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1989 note1 identifies The Structure of Scientific Revolutions(1962) and expressly limits paradigm here to a conceptual framework and/or its presuppositions. This records acknowledged terminology with an explicit departure, not adoption of Kuhn’s full theory or proof of a formative lineage. Kuhn’s original book unread.
primary_locators: 1989 printed460 note1; article’s use of paradigm460,464.

proposals.relationship: Higham draws on E. P. Thompson’s formulation of independent intellectual territory to explain why dissenting historians need a sustaining community.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1989 printed462 names E.P.Thompson and quotes the need for journals and centers belonging to the community. This conceptual support sits within Higham’s argument about the isolation of radical scholarship; no organizational collaboration or exclusive influence is inferred. Note4 identifies Tocqueville for the preceding conformity argument and does not supply the Thompson source; its title/date remain unresolved and the original unread.
primary_locators: 1989 printed462 first paragraph, sentence beginning Perhaps even more than elsewhere, with body attribution E.P.Thompson; note4 distinction.

proposals.relationship: Higham uses Black Reconstruction as an important example for distinguishing racial exclusion of a scholar from the uneven scholarly reception of radical historical work.
proposals.evidence_note: Own1989 printed461/n3 ranks DuBois and Curti’s1935 works highly, describes white scholars’ use of DuBois’s evidence despite rejecting his Marxism, and makes that distinction part of his reply to Wiener. Higham’s account is attributed rather than independently certified;462 also makes an additional claim about DuBois’s lack of disciples, not independently verified here, which this edge does not adopt as fact or convert into a personal criticism. Curti, Beale and Armstead Robinson retain their separate credit; cited originals unread.
primary_locators: 1989 printed461 paragraphs beginning Prior to1965 / The problem of reception; note3;462 paragraph beginning Curti and DuBois.

proposals.relationship: Higham draws, through Ian Tyrrell’s account, on Genovese’s work as one example of the stronger interpretive resources of American radical scholarship in the1960s.
proposals.evidence_note: Explicit named mediation: Higham1989,461/n2 credits Ian Tyrrell’s The Absent Marx and names Genovese jointly with Gabriel Kolko and Barrington Moore,Jr. Higham says their example does not by itself explain the collective breakthrough. His465–466/n10 separately discusses Elkins and Tannenbaum as resources for Genovese and identifies The Political Economy of Slavery(1965). No sole-source lineage or fresh reading of Tyrrell/Genovese originals is claimed.
primary_locators: 1989 printed461 opening/n2;465 final paragraph continued466 and note10.
